newsitem.title: USA: Avalanche of bids to enroll in U.S. land reserve.
newsitem.headline: Avalanche of bids to enroll in U.S. land reserve.

text.p: Farmers offered a mammoth 25.6 million acres (10.4 million hectares) -- far more than expected -- for the Conservation Reserve, the U.S. Agriculture Department said Tuesday, buckling down to deciding which to accept.
Up to 21 million acres could be accepted but officials, led by Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, say they will enroll the most fragile land. There is no quota, they say.
By mid-June, farmers will be told if their land is accepted.

Glickman said in a statement the vast pool of offers received during March -- about 301,650 bids covering 25.6 million acres -- would give his department the chance to ferret out land with the greatest environmental benefit.
"That helps us get the biggest bang for the taxpayers' buck," he said.

Skeptics in the environmental and agribusiness sectors fear the job will be fumbled in the crush of work. They say the department erred at the start by making too much land eligible for consideration and was under political pressure to keep enrollment high in the arid, wheat-growing Great Plains.
"Now comes the hard work on the part of (the department)," Bob Peterson, spokesman for the Coalition for a Competitive Food and Agriculture System, said, referring to the winnowing process.
The coalition says "good productive land should not be locked up another 10 years."
"I hope they resist the temptation to move too quickly," said Ken Cook of the Environmental Working Group. "It's even more important to do it right."

Created in 1985, the Conservation Reserve pays an annual rent to farmers who take fragile land out of production for 10 years in order to protect water purity, reduce soil erosion and enhance wildlife habitat.

Congress has limited enrollment to a maximum of 36.4 million acres, so this year's sign-up, by involving up to two-thirds of the land, could shape the program for a decade to come. Contracts expire this fall on 21.5 million acres.

Farmers submitted bids to re-enroll about 18 million acres under contract and to enroll eight million new acres. Texas led the nation in acreage offered with 3.4 million, followed by North Dakota with 2.5 million acres and Montana with 2.3 million acres.
The Agriculture Department said it would assess offers under a formula that considered the annual rent requested by a farmer and the environmental benefits that would be gained.
At present, wheat and feed grain land dominate enrollment.
